blocks.text: The lung is an organ of the respiratory system, even and asymmetrical, it represents the seat of gas exchanges (hematosis), and is surrounded by a serous envelope, the pleura.

1- Situation The lungs are located in the thoracic cavity, they occupy the pleuropulmonary cavities on either side of the mediastinum. 2- Consistency and color The lung is smooth, shiny pink in children, pinkish gray in adults and bluish in the elderly. The lung is spongy, soft and elastic. 3- Dimensions Length: 25cm Antero-posterior diameter: 18cm Transverse diameter: 7 to 10cm 4- Weight: The weight in humans is 700g for the right lung and 650g for the left lung. In women the weight is 550g for the right lung and 450g for the left lung. Normal inspiratory capacity is equal to 3500 cm3. The forced inspiratory capacity is equal to 5000 cm3. 5- Shape The lung has the shape of a half-cone (triangular pyramid) with three faces: external, internal and lower, three edges: anterior, posterior and lower and a summit or apex. External configuration a-External face This is the costal face, it is rounded, convex. It molds to the deep side of the rib cage and presents the imprints of the ribs. The right lung marked by the presence of two fissures: an oblique fissure (the large fissure) and a horizontal fissure (the small fissure). On the other hand, the left lung presents a single oblique fissure. b-Internal face This is the mediastinal face, it is concave, presents in its middle part the pulmonary hilum. The hilum is oval on the right and triangular on the left, it continues downwards by the triangular ligament. At its level, the different elements of the pulmonary pedicle flourish, which are of two types: -Nourishing elements: formed by the arteries, veins, lymphatics and bronchial nerves. -Functional elements (participating in hematosis): represented by the main bronchi, the pulmonary artery, the pulmonary veins (two right and two left) The mediastinal face present on its surface the imprints of the anatomical elements of the neighborhoods. The left lung shows the imprints of the aortic arch, the thoracic aorta, the left subclavian artery and the heart. The right lung presents the imprints of the heart (right atrium), the superior vena cava SVC, the brachiocephalic arterial trunk, the brachiocephalic venous trunk, and the arch of the azygos vein.

c- Diaphragmatic face The diaphragmatic face represents the base of the lung. It is concave and molds to the diaphragm, and responds through it to the organs of the upper mesocolic level of the abdominal cavity. It is covered by the diaphragmatic pleura. d- Summit Also called the apex of the lung, it is rounded and extends beyond the upper orifice of the thorax. e- Anterior edge The anterior edge separates the medial and lateral faces in front. On the left lung: it has a large notch: the cardiac incision. f- Posterior edge The posterior edge separates the two medial and lateral faces behind, it is not very marked. g- Lower edge Or circumferential edge, it circumscribes the base of the lung. Segmentation of the right lung The right lung is divided by the two oblique and transverse fissures into three lobes: upper, middle and lower. Each lobe is subdivided into segments. -The upper lobe is subdivided into three segments: apical segment, dorsal segment, and ventral segment. -The middle lobe is subdivided into two segments: lateral segment and medial segment. -The lower lobe describes five lobes: apical segment of the lower lobe or Fowler's, baso-medial or paracardiac segment, ventro-basal segment, latero-basal segment and dorso-basal or end-basal segment.

1-Segmentation of the left lung The left lung is divided by a single fissure into two upper and lower lobes. The upper lobe is divided into two groups: upper group or culmen which contains the apical segment, the dorsal segment and the ventral segment and a lower group or lingula which contains two segments: upper or cranial segment and lower or caudal segment. Finally, the lower lobe presents a segmentation identical to that of the lower lobe of the right lung.

Bronchial arteries Of very variable origin, generally
Two in number on the left, upper, and lower, arising directly from the descending thoracic aorta
one on the right, arising from the first posterior and right intercostal artery
travel along the posterior surface of the right main bronchus,

enter the lung and irrigate it The Bronchial veins Venous drainage is via anterior and posterior veins, which drain to the right towards the vein azygos and to the left towards the accessory hemi azygos. The lymphatic vessels are made up of two systems, one superficial, pleural, the other deep, following the bronchial tree and the pulmonary vessels. These two systems have anastomoses at the level of the pulmonary hilum. Each lung has three lymphatic drainage territories: upper, middle and lower.
The superficial lymphatic vessels of the lung, as well as those of the visceral pleura, ? and the deep lymphatic vessels lead to the tracheobronchial lymph nodes,
The collectors which leave from them constitute two chains on each side, one anterior mediastinal, the other posterior constituted by the tracheal lymph nodes

blocks.text: Functional vascularization provided by the pulmonary artery It is the arterial trunk which carries venous blood towards the lungs constituting the small circulation, it detaches from the base of the right ventricle, measuring 5 cm in length, it divides into two branches, the right and left pulmonary arteries. The right pulmonary artery Intended for the right lung, it is larger than the left, 5 cm long and 22 mm in diameter. It crosses the mediastinum, penetrates the hilum of the right lung, passes above the middle lobar bronchus, then descends along the lower lobar bronchus and ends at the posterior surface of the posterior basal segmental bronchus. Its collateral branches are satellites of the bronchi and arise along the lecturee of the artery. The left pulmonary artery Intended for the left lung. It crosses the left main bronchus, penetrates the pulmonary hilum above the upper lobar bronchus, it ends at the posterior surface of the posterior basal segmental bronchus. Its collateral branches are satellites of the bronchi and arise along the lecturee of the artery. Innervation
